content: Acute sinusitis is characterized by inflammation and swelling of the nasal and paranasal mucous membranes, often leading to symptoms such as facial pain and nasal congestion. These symptoms can significantly impair daily functioning and quality of life, making acute sinusitis a common reason for patients to seek medical care. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of systemic corticosteroids on clinical outcomes, including symptom resolution, adverse effects, and relapse rates, in both children and adults with acute sinusitis. The study compared systemic corticosteroids to placebo or standard clinical care. The researchers conducted a systematic search of databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Five RCTs involving a total of 1,193 adult participants met the inclusion criteria. The methodological quality of the trials was assessed as moderate in four studies and high in one study. Acute sinusitis was diagnosed clinically in all trials, with three trials also incorporating radiological assessments as part of their inclusion criteria. Participants in the trials were assigned to receive either oral corticosteroids (prednisone doses ranging from 24 mg to 80 mg daily or betamethasone 1 mg daily) or a control treatment (placebo in four trials and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) in one trial). In four of the trials, antibiotics were prescribed in addition to the corticosteroids or control treatment, while one trial investigated corticosteroids as a monotherapy. When data from the five trials were combined, it was found that participants treated with oral corticosteroids were more likely to experience short-term symptom resolution or improvement compared to those receiving the control treatment. Specifically, at days three to seven, the risk ratio (RR) was 1.3 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.1 to 1.6), with a risk difference (RD) of 17% (95% CI 6% to 29%). At days four to 14, the RR was 1.2 (95% CI 1.0 to 1.5), with an RD of 14% (95% CI 1% to 27%). A sensitivity analysis that included only the four trials using placebo as the control treatment showed similar results but with a smaller effect size. At days three to seven, the RR was 1.2 (95% CI 1.1 to 1.3), with an RD of 11% (95% CI 4% to 17%). At days four to 14, the RR was 1.1 (95% CI 1.0 to 1.2), with an RD of 8% (95% CI 2% to 13%). However, there was significant statistical heterogeneity in many of the analyses. Subgroup analyses indicated that corticosteroid monotherapy did not provide any significant benefit. Additionally, a scenario analysis suggested that missing outcome data from the trials could have introduced attrition bias. In a worst-case scenario, no statistically significant benefit of oral corticosteroids was observed. None of the trials reported data on relapse or recurrence rates. The reported side effects of oral corticosteroids were mild, including nausea, vomiting, and gastric complaints, and these did not differ significantly from the side effects reported in the placebo groups. In conclusion, oral corticosteroids as a monotherapy appear to be ineffective for treating acute sinusitis in adults. The current evidence on the use of oral corticosteroids as an adjunct to antibiotics is limited, with most trials conducted in secondary care settings and a significant risk of bias. The available data suggest that oral corticosteroids, when combined with antibiotics, may provide modest short-term symptom relief in acute sinusitis, with a number needed to treat (NNT) of seven for symptom resolution or improvement. However, further large-scale trials in primary care settings are needed to determine whether oral corticosteroids offer additional benefits over antibiotics alone in the treatment of acute sinusitis.
